messages.author: 15072e0cb1dd13d7
messages.subject: 'Tidy data' paper
parts:
http://vita.had.co.nz/papers/tidy-data.pdf

I just read the pre-published version of 'Tidy data'.  Thank you, Prof. Wickham for making it available!  I especially appreciated several sections:

1) the affirmation that about 80% of the time is spent cleaning the data.  I work from home for a small epidemiology academic research group and do not interact with other research assistants and data analysts nearly as much as I'd like.  It had the "I'm not the only one!" effect on me and was heartening.

2) translation of population research terms into computer science terms since I do find a lot of the advice on good data and R programming practices on the web comes from programmers.

3) The section on fixed and measured variables did send me off on tangential thoughts about how valid that dichotomy is in observational research....hmmm

4) reassured me that my preference for 'long' tables (person.period) over wide tables is good.  QUESTION: However, using 'melt' a few days ago brought up a question for which I have not found an answer on the web.  I was revising my data cleaning script for a project because we got an update in the data.  I thought I would neatly rename and label my variables and factors at the beginning (with Hmisc).  To my dismay I found 'melt' and sqldf don't like variable labels, sqldf is a pain when variable names contain dots... Any advice?

5) My confusion and frustration with untidy output such as 'table' is not unfounded.  Although getting better with mutli-dimensional lists, I love to get things into a flat  table (or related tables) format.

6) Finally, the reassurance that relational databases and their governing principles offer applicable lessons.  I had started to wonder--with all the talk on the web of Hadoop, etc and the paucity of advice on new tools for traditional data structures--whether the RDBMS model was on its way out. 

"the tools we use strongly inﬂuence the way we think"---very true.  I wondered if starting with MS Access, sql and SAS had limited a broader understanding of 'data' that would be useful in R (and in general).

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: 'Tidy data' paper
parts:
Hi Tanya,

Glad that you found it helpful, and thanks for letting me know.

Unfortunately I've rarely worked with datasets that have so many
variables that I don't remember what they all mean, so I've never used
tools like labels. I would probably keep the mapping between variable
names and labels in its own vector so you could easily reapply it
after other transformations lose it.

Hadley
